TikTok post-path capture · jailbroken iPhone X · 14 August 2026

Everything TikTok reads when you post

We hooked the app with Frida and posted fourteen files, one per session, each with a deliberately different history. Two separate investigations came out of it — one for video, one for photos — and they do not reach the same conclusion, so they are kept apart here.

Nine clips: generated, downloaded, filmed on the phone, injected with fake metadata, and AI-generated. TikTok read every provenance field each file carried, invented nothing for the files that had none, and validated nothing on the file that lied. None of it survived TikTok’s own re-encode — but on the AI clip it added a label of its own. And a clip edited outside the app can be made to read exactly like camera footage.

Read this before the table

Three limits on what this proves

  • It shows what TikTok reads, never what TikTok concludes. Every row is a call the app made. Nothing here shows a score, a threshold, or a ranking effect. Any claim that a metadata rewrite moves reach is outside this evidence.
  • Only clip 6 (CANARY) was traced past the encoder. It is the one arm with a re-encode dump. For the other seven we can say what was read, not what survived.
  • The AI label is confirmed. What removes it is not. Clip 7 (AI) got aigc_info written into its export. Clips 8 (AI STRIPPED) and 9 (NATIVIZED) carry the same footage and did not — and that absence is trustworthy, because the value is recorded even where key names are not. But both of those also went through a different encoder path (isFastImport 1 against clip 7’s 0), so we changed two things at once and cannot say which one dropped the label.
  • We never saw the uploaded bytes. The TLS hook captured the CDN request headers — 1 774 bytes announcing Content-Length: 34384 — but none of that 34 KB body. The re-encode feeding it is measured clean, so the upload almost certainly is too, but that last step is inference, not observation. A second publish call (/aweme/v1/aweme/post/) was never seen either: attaching the hook killed the app both times, ~51s in, right after the success haptic.

What they got from each clip

One clip per emptied camera roll, one Frida session each, so no value below is contaminated by a neighbouring file. A dash means the field was not on that file — and TikTok did not invent it. The first seven groups are the ones that carry the argument; the rest of what it touched follows underneath, so the table is the whole set rather than a selection from it.

Clip 8 (AI STRIPPED) is blended. Its Recents still held four clips, so the picker deep-walked all of them and its INPUT column mixes files — including a leftover TikTok export, which is why a TEEditor JSON string shows up under device software. Only its written row is attributable to the clip that was posted. Every other column had exactly one item in Recents.

On the AI-label row, a dash is real evidence. Most exports report their fields as numbered keys rather than names, but the rig records the value either way — and the string aigc_label_type appears in exactly one export across all nine clips.

Two rows that look like findings and are not. The audio encoder string (id3/TSSE) tracks the backing-music file TikTok loads rather than your video, so clips sharing a track share the value. The itsk block is TikTok’s own encoder writing to itself. Both are listed because the table claims to be complete, not because they say anything about the clip you posted.

Still deliberately out: thumbnail properties, which are interface bitmaps rather than your video, and filesystem dates, which cover TikTok’s own drafts and exports as well as your file. Both are in the ledger.

Read clip 2 (STAMPED) against clip 6 (CANARY). Both were faked by hand. Clip 2 put its GPS in an XMP packet and TikTok read that packet as an opaque blob, parsing no coordinate. Clip 6 put the same kind of value in a QuickTime key and it came back 18 times. Same rig, one container apart.

Every distinct thing read across the six sessions, grouped by what it reveals. The bar is how often it was read, not how many fields there are — TikTok re-polls the whole metadata set continuously while you sit on the compose screen.

Ordered by what it gives away, not by how loud it is. Note the bars: the four blocks that identify you are the quietest things TikTok reads — thumbnails and library dimensions dominate the volume and are identical whoever posts. A few hundred quiet reads are the whole exposure.

Where it goes, and where it dies

Traced on clip 6 (CANARY), the only arm with dumps downstream of the picker. Three of the four stages are measured. The fourth is where the instrumentation ran out.

0survive the rebuildthe streams are copied untouched and the container is rebuilt without them

?on the wirenever captured — we logged the request headers, not the 34 KB body
Exposure is on-deviceThe picker and the encoder read the file in full. That is where your camera location and device identity are exposed — to the app, on the handset, before anything is sent.Measured directly, on all six clips.Confirmed
The re-encode drops all of itThe file TikTok built for upload, pulled back off the phone, holds none of the ten fields. What it holds instead is TikTok’s own block.Hw, Bitrate, Copyright, Software (a TEEditor JSON blob), Source, Encoder=Lavf57.71.100 — nine keys, none of them yours.Confirmed
The upload itself is unmeasuredThe TLS hook logged the CDN request headers and stopped. We have the declared Content-Length: 34384 but not one byte of that payload, so the wire capture cannot say what it contained.The re-encode feeding it is clean, which makes a clean upload very likely — but that is inference, not observation. A separate aweme_v1 JSON call was never seen at all.Open

The one thing TikTok adds: an AI label

Every field so far was something TikTok took. Clip 7 (AI) is the opposite. It is an AI-generator export carrying no C2PA, no Sora or OpenAI string, nothing that announces what made it — and TikTok still wrote a label into the file it produced.

aigc_infoWritten into the export at 22.5s, read back 2×. The value is {"aigc_label_type":2}.It appears in no other arm. A string search across all eight sessions finds aigc_label_type only here and in the follow-up that re-read this same file.Confirmed
Nothing in the source declared itThe clip carried Lavf58.76.100 and nothing else. No C2PA manifest, no provenance sidecar, no generator name.So the label was not copied forward from the file. TikTok decided it some other way — from the pixels, from the upload context, or from something we cannot see on the handset.Unexplained
The Sora demo sat beside itA public OpenAI Sora clip (IMG_0028, 29.7 MB) was in the same camera roll and got picker-walked, but it was not the posted file.Worth noting for a different reason: its XMP carries an After Effects project path from an OpenAI shared drive. Real provenance leaks are usually this boring.Context

Both panels are the block TikTok wrote into its own export. Clip 7 named its fields; clip 8 numbered them. Either way the values are captured, and aigc_label_type is in only one of them. What stays open is why: the clip that got labelled is also the only one TikTok fully re-encoded, so stripping the file and taking a different encoder path are still confounded.

How to make a clip look like a real iPhone recording

Clip 5 (CAMERA) is the reference implementation: a genuine iPhone X capture, so whatever it carries is by definition what a legitimate file looks like. Clip 6 (CANARY) proves TikTok checks none of it for plausibility — arbitrary strings came back verbatim. So the job is to match the shape, not to be convincing.

What a real iPhone X file carries

Makealways the string AppleApple
Modelthe marketing name, not the identifieriPhone X
Softwarethe iOS build the clip was shot on16.7.16
CreationDatelocal time with a real UTC offset2026:08:14 19:31:34+03:00
GPSCoordinateslat, lon, altitude — where you filmed54.6389 24.9351 161.972
LocationAccuracyHorizontalmetres of GPS uncertainty35.0

What gives a fake away anyway

CodeciPhone shoots HEVC (hvc1). A stamped ffmpeg clip is usually H.264 (avc1) and the mismatch is visible in the same read.
Track layoutThe real capture carries five tracks — video, audio and three timed-metadata tracks. exiftool cannot add those.
Photos sourceTypeEvery file you import reads as user-library, whatever its atoms say. Only a clip actually recorded on the device is a camera original.
Resolution and rate1920×1080 at 30fps for this model. A 720×1280 testcard with an Apple stamp contradicts itself.
the stamp
# what a real iPhone X recording carries, reproduced onto any clip
exiftool -overwrite_original \
  -Keys:Make="Apple" \
  -Keys:Model="iPhone X" \
  -Keys:Software="16.7.16" \
  -Keys:CreationDate="2026:08:14 19:31:34+03:00" \
  -Keys:GPSCoordinates="54.6389, 24.9351, 161.972" \
  -Keys:LocationAccuracyHorizontal="35.0" \
  clip.mov

# the picture has to match the story: iPhone shoots HEVC, not H.264
ffmpeg -i clip.mov -c:v hevc_videotoolbox -tag:v hvc1 \
  -s 1920x1080 -r 30 -c:a aac out.mov
Use Keys, never XMPQuickTime Keys: is the container TikTok parses. XMP is read as an opaque blob and no value is extracted from it.Clip 2 (STAMPED) wrote GPS to XMP only and TikTok never produced a coordinate. Clip 6 (CANARY) wrote it to Keys and got read 18 times.The whole trick
GPSCoordinates, not GPSLatitudeexiftool has no Keys:LocationISO6709. Keys:GPSCoordinates is the tag that lands as the mdta ISO 6709 atom the app actually reads.Easy to miss
Re-check after the Photos importPhotos rewrites imported files. Clip 2 (STAMPED) went in at 16 524 B and came back stripped to about 9 459 B, which silently invalidates your stamp.Pull the file back off the device and re-dump before you trust it. The canary survived intact, which is why clip 6 is usable.Verify
Values need not be realTikTok range-checked nothing. CANARYMK-7F3A and a GPS reading of 11.1111, 22.2222 were both accepted and read back unchanged.Proven

Left: the clip after Photos imported it — the stamp is intact, so Photos is not what destroyed it. Right: what TikTok built for upload. Same clip, one encoder apart.

Can a clip edited somewhere else pass as a native capture?

The in-app editor is limited, so the practical question is whether a clip cut in real software can be restamped to read the way camera footage reads. Arm 9 is that test: the AI clip from arm 7, re-encoded and stamped from a genuine capture taken on the same phone minutes earlier, posted into an emptied camera roll so every read is attributable.

Reproduced by nativize.py in the repo: it copies every field from a real capture, re-encodes to hvc1 at the reference’s size and rate, strips anything the reference lacks, then diffs the result against it.

Does it do this to clips as well?

Every clip on this page was posted from an emptied camera roll, one file at a time. That is the one condition under which a sweep of the roll is invisible, so the question went unanswered for nine arms. Two clips settle it: each carries a canary the other does not, and each was posted in its own session.

SessionPostedRead its own canaryRead the other clip’sDistinct locations read
clip Agreen clipreadread5
clip Bpurple clipreadread5

Both directions, same answer. Posting either clip, TikTok read the other one — and three of the phone’s real recordings alongside it, visible as five distinct coordinates in a roll that held five clips. Video sweeps the camera roll exactly as the photo picker does, so nothing about the clip findings is confined to the file you chose.

This also retires an assumption. Clip 8 showed picker-walk values in its column and was marked blended as a defect of setup. It was not a defect; it was this behaviour, showing up by accident a dozen arms before anyone tested for it.

The part of a recording nothing on this page could see

A photo carries a hundred fields and a recording carries six. That gap looked like a finding for most of this audit, and it was not: it was the instrument. Everything above reads a file’s container metadata, and a recording keeps almost nothing there. What it keeps instead is three timed-metadata tracks running the full length of the clip, and they declare this:

Key declared in the mebx tracksWhat it holds
com.apple.quicktime.detected-facethat a face was found, per frame
com.apple.quicktime.detected-face.boundswhere in the frame it sat
com.apple.quicktime.detected-face.face-idan identifier for that face across the clip
com.apple.quicktime.detected-face.roll-anglehow far the head was tilted
com.apple.quicktime.detected-face.yaw-anglehow far it was turned
com.apple.quicktime.live-photo-infoper-frame Live Photo state
com.apple.quicktime.video-orientationorientation, per frame

exiftool reports 822 tags on a real recording when told to open the embedded tracks, against 200 when not — and it can only decode one of the three. A 6.8-second clip holds 203 per-frame samples in that one track alone. Your phone writes this into every recording it makes, whether or not anything ever reads it.

TikTok neither reads it nor uploads it

Two ways to reach those samples exist: an AVAssetReader over the metadata track, or AVPlayerItemMetadataOutput. Both were hooked and both stayed silent across a complete post — picker, compose, encode and upload. And the file TikTok actually sends is its own re-encode, which was pulled off the phone and compared:

 TracksmebxApple keys
the recording you posted5314, including every face key
what TikTok uploaded202, both written by TikTok

The re-encode drops to video and audio and keeps nothing else. This is measured rather than inferred, which matters: the earlier re-encode on this page came from a synthetic clip that never had metadata tracks to lose, so it could not tell a strip apart from an absence. This input had three and the output has none.

It is not a re-encode. It is a rebuild.

Losing metadata to a transcode would be collateral damage. This is not that. The same post that answered the face question also gave the first side-by-side of a real recording against the file TikTok made from it, and the picture is unambiguous:

 CodecSizeFrame rateMedia payload
your recordinghvc11920×108030.007 fps6 677 964 B
what TikTok uploadedhvc11920×108030.007 fps6 648 714 B

30.007 is the tell. No encoder produces that — a real transcode lands on exactly 30. It survives, hvc1 survives where most platforms convert HEVC to H.264, and the media payload comes out 0.4% smaller. TikTok’s own export agrees, writing te_is_reencode: 0 and isFastImport: 1 into the file.

29 250 bytes were removed, and that is essentially the three metadata tracks. Your video and audio are copied through untouched. What TikTok does is rebuild the container around them without your Keys atoms and without the timed-metadata tracks — so the stripping is a decision, not a side effect of compression. Same outcome as a re-encode would give, arrived at deliberately.

Two things it writes every time and that are not new to this run: the movie-header dates are zeroed to 0000:00:00, and a 32-character Copyright hash is stamped in. The older canary export carries both.

Where it does go

The face data is Apple’s, not TikTok’s, and it is in the file on the phone. Anything that takes the original bytes rather than a re-encode carries it along — AirDrop, email, a cloud drive that stores what it is given, a backup. TikTok is the case that was measured here, and TikTok strips it. That says nothing about anywhere else the same file goes.

What a real recording is shaped like

A recording’s shape is not one shape

Everything else on this page is metadata. This is structure — how many tracks the file has and what each one is for — and it has to be right before any value inside it matters.

RecordingFrame rateTracksLayout
IMG_0047.MOV30.007 fps5vide, soun, meta, meta, meta
IMG_0049.MOV240.17 fps2vide, soun
IMG_0059.MOV30 fps5vide, soun, meta, meta, meta

Slow motion drops the metadata tracks entirely. A normal 1080p30 capture carries five tracks — video, audio and three timed-metadata (mebx) tracks holding per-frame gyroscope and exposure data. A 240 fps capture carries two. So there is no single native shape to imitate; there is a shape per recording mode, and a forgery has to match the one it claims to be.

That has a practical consequence for the playbook above. Those mebx tracks are the one part ffmpeg cannot write — it emits a plain sample table where a real recording has proper mebx sample entries, which is why rebuilding one convincingly looked like it needed AVAssetWriter on the device. A slow-motion clip has none to rebuild.

Five stills, posted the same way. The video finding was that TikTok takes everything on the file you post. The photo finding is worse than that, and it is not the same claim: the picker reads the metadata of every image in the roll, including the ones you never touch.

That single decision is what exposed the finding below; had they shared an id, as they were first built, every hit would have looked like the file just posted and there would have been nothing to see.

On photos, XMP is parsed — the opposite of video

Photo 4 carries no EXIF, no IFD0, no GPS block at all. Its make and coordinates exist only inside an XMP packet. TikTok read them anyway, because ImageIO folds XMP into the same {TIFF} and {GPS} dictionaries it fills from EXIF. AVFoundation does not do this for video, which is why clip 2’s XMP stayed an opaque blob. The video playbook rule does not carry over.

Photo 2 is the only column with a full house, because it is the only genuine capture. Lens, exposure, sub-second timing, compass bearing and the Apple block are things a camera writes and a forgery has to reproduce — and photo 3, built from that very image, has the entire camera-settings group empty. That gap is the tell.

The three UUIDs in the Apple block are the sharpest thing here. A coordinate can be faked and a timestamp moved, but ContentIdentifier and PhotoIdentifier exist to be unique to one shot. Copying a real maker note onto other files — the obvious way to make a photo look camera-shot — stamps every one of them with the same supposedly-unique id.

What the stills runs do not show

  • No upload body was captured on any of the five. Between three and seven request bodies per run, all of it launch telemetry — nothing from the post itself. What reaches the CDN for a photo is unmeasured, exactly as it is for the clips.
  • Reads are attributed by value, not by file handle. The rig records values per tag key with no note of which file they came from, so the claim that a non-selected photo was read rests on its unique canary appearing in the session. Sound here because every arm differs — but inference from the value set, not a per-file trace. It is also why the values above are read back off the files rather than taken from the capture.
  • Answered, below: the sweep is bounded. These runs used a roll of eight, which is entirely inside the bound, so every figure above stands. A separate run with three hundred files found the reach and it is nearer sixty than three hundred.
  • Photos 2 and 3 are not in the repository. They are a real capture and a restamped copy of it: personal pixels, home GPS, and maker-note UUIDs.

Fields that cannot be filled in independently

Knowing which fields move is not enough to write one. Several are two spellings of a single quantity, or dates that have to agree, or counters that have to keep counting. Get one of those wrong and the file is inconsistent with itself — wrong by arithmetic, visible without any reference file to compare against.

  • ShutterSpeedValue and ApertureValue are the other two spellings of ExposureTime and FNumber. Stored as APEX, the same quantities in log form. They must agree — and, because APEX is a rational that does not round-trip exactly, they must agree inexactly. On a real capture the pair reads 0.25 against 0.249994. Writing both from one float gives exact equality, which no genuine file has.
  • GPSDateStamp has to be the same day as DateTimeOriginal. Two dates in two different blocks describing one moment. Likewise the three OffsetTime spellings, which all have to carry the same timezone.
  • RunTimeValue is a nanosecond counter since the phone last booted. It moves every shot while RunTimeEpoch, RunTimeScale and RunTimeFlags hold still, so across a set of photos it has to increase monotonically and by roughly the gaps between the timestamps being claimed.
  • AccelerationVector is the accelerometer reading at the moment of capture. It has to be consistent with the Orientation on the same file. A portrait photo whose gravity vector says landscape is contradicting itself.
  • The lens is a bundle, not a field. The two rear cameras report 4mm f/1.8 and 6mm f/2.4, so LensModel, FNumber, FocalLength and ApertureValue move together. A file pairing a 4 mm focal length with f/2.4 describes a camera that does not exist.
  • The frame is always landscape. ExifImageWidth and ExifImageHeight never move: every capture is stored 4032×3024 and a portrait photo is expressed purely as Orientation 6 — the same trick a real recording uses when it stores video landscape with a rotation matrix.

All of these held on all three captures, so a forgery has to hold them too. The check is in analyze_stills_variance.py. Values of identifying fields are never printed — that a coordinate or a UUID varies is the finding, what it says is not — and the photographs themselves stay out of the repository.

Where the sweep stops

Everything above was measured in a roll of five to eight photos, which is small enough that reading all of it proves nothing about a real library. Three hundred stills went in, each carrying its own index twice over — once as a name a search finds, once as a coordinate that sorts — and one unrelated file was posted.

54of 300 read
246never touched
~63assets deep it reaches
9gaps inside that block

The sweep is bounded. It read the newest 54 files in the roll and stopped. The remaining 246 were sitting in the same library, indexed and available, and were never touched. Both channels agree on the figure independently, which is the check that stops a silent failure looking like a bound.

What a bound does and does not buy you

  • Only the top of the roll is exposed. Roughly 63 assets deep, on this handset in this session. Below that, files cost nothing however many there are.
  • It is not a hiding place. A roll whose newest 63 items are all the same kind of file is fully exposed no matter how large the library is. Burial under volume does not work; keeping the top of the roll coherent does.
  • 9 gaps sit inside the block that was read. So this is a neighbourhood rather than a constant, and a number to design margin around rather than to trust exactly.
  • Nobody scrolled. The posted file was picked immediately, so this measures the default reach of opening the picker. A user who scrolls renders more of the grid, and there is no reason to think the bound survives that.

How it was measured

The rule that keeps it clean

One clip per emptied camera rollOpening the picker makes TikTok stat and deep-walk every visible asset, so a library with five clips produces one log holding all five clips' metadata with no way to split it. Every session below had exactly one item.
Read-only, spawn not attachThe observer hooks reads and never injects to post. Posting is done by hand on the device.
562 rows are 423 factsAVFoundation exposes the same atom under six format identifiers, so one value on the file logs up to six times. The ledger collapses on (phase, atom, value) and keeps the keyspaces. Nothing is discarded.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location. The app made no location calls this run, which is not proof it never asks,
    only that it did not while being watched.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-1-solo\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-1-solo\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location. The app made no location calls this run, which is not proof it never asks,
    only that it did not while being watched.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-2-solo\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-2-solo\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location. The app made no location calls this run, which is not proof it never asks,
    only that it did not while being watched.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-3-sintel\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-3-sintel\audit.json.

  │     The tell is which fields came back (ColorModel, DPIHeight, DPIWidth, Depth,          │
  │     HasAlpha, IsIndexed, ...): orientation, pixel geometry and camera model are what     │
  │     a decoder wants, a GPS or a full EXIF block is what a harvester wants.               │
  │   ▸ No picker of either kind opened, but a capture session did, so the media came        │
  │     from the in-app camera rather than from your library.                                │
  │   ▸ No upload task was created, so nothing left through Apple's networking. TikTok       │
  │     publishes through its own uploader, and the only hook that can see those bytes       │
  │     is the tls probe, which samples for 600ms at a time. Run with -Full and publish      │
  │     while a probe window is live, or treat the upload itself as out of reach.            │
  │   ▸ 3 post-path hooks did not attach at all: AVAssetWriter, AVURLAsset, PHAsset.         │
  │     Everything above is blind to those.                                                  │
  ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location. The app made no location calls this run, which is not proof it never asks,
    only that it did not while being watched.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-4-bunny\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-4-bunny\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location asked of the OS. The app made no CLLocationManager calls, but it DID read a
    position out of a media file, which is listed above and needs no permission. Absence
    here is not absence of location.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-5-camera\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-5-camera\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Anything the touch probe would have caught. It armed correctly and saw ZERO calls, which
    means the app was idle in those windows, not that it never does these things. Raw-socket
    and TLS work clusters in the first ten seconds, which is under the launch watchdog and
    cannot be sampled safely. Scroll the feed while the probes run, or use -Attach on an app
    you are already using.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location asked of the OS. The app made no CLLocationManager calls, but it DID read a
    position out of a media file, which is listed above and needs no permission. Absence
    here is not absence of location.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-6-canary-2\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-6-canary-2\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location. The app made no location calls this run, which is not proof it never asks,
    only that it did not while being watched.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-8-ai-2\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-8-ai-2\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location. The app made no location calls this run, which is not proof it never asks,
    only that it did not while being watched.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-9-stripped\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-9-stripped\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Anything the touch probe would have caught. It armed correctly and saw ZERO calls, which
    means the app was idle in those windows, not that it never does these things. Raw-socket
    and TLS work clusters in the first ten seconds, which is under the launch watchdog and
    cannot be sampled safely. Scroll the feed while the probes run, or use -Attach on an app
    you are already using.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location asked of the OS. The app made no CLLocationManager calls, but it DID read a
    position out of a media file, which is listed above and needs no permission. Absence
    here is not absence of location.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-11-nativized-solo\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-11-nativized-solo\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Most of what the touch probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at a
    time, 12 passes in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Exact counts for getenv reads. It stopped counting at 6000 to keep the app responsive,
    so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Exact counts for track format description reads. It stopped counting at 60 to keep the
    app responsive, so that number is a floor and the real one is higher.
  ▸ Rates for 31 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached:
    AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset -
    commonMetadata (not implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented
    by this class), PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class). A hook that
    failed and a mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them
    is a finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location asked of the OS. The app made no CLLocationManager calls, but it DID read a
    position out of a media file, which is listed above and needs no permission. Absence
    here is not absence of location.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
  ▸ Full transcript in runs\unique-10-nativized\session.log, machine-readable in
    runs\unique-10-nativized\audit.json.

  not shown
  ▸ Anything after 51.4s. iOS killed the app there, so the remaining 129s of the window
    recorded nothing and no absence below should be read as proof.
  ▸ The launch sequence. This run attached to an app that was already open, which is what
    keeps iOS from killing it, but the first seconds of a cold start are where most
    identifier reads happen.
  ▸ Most of what the publish probe could have seen. Each attaches for well under a second at
    a time, 1 pass in this run, because keeping them on is what made iOS kill the app. They
    prove a mechanism is used, never how often.
  ▸ Anything the publish probe would have caught. It armed correctly and saw ZERO calls,
    which means the app was idle in those windows, not that it never does these things.
    Raw-socket and TLS work clusters in the first ten seconds, which is under the launch
    watchdog and cannot be sampled safely. Scroll the feed while the probes run, or use
    -Attach on an app you are already using.
  ▸ Rates for 28 other hooks. They ran for a fixed slice of time rather than to a call
    limit, so their counts are what happened in that slice and imply nothing about the rest
    of the run.
  ▸ Anything these post-path hooks would have caught, because they never attached: AVAsset -
    commonMetadata (attach threw: Error: unable to intercept function at 0x15cea8970; please
    file a bug), AVAsset - metadata (attach threw: Error: unable to intercept function at
    0x15cea8850; please file a bug), AVAssetWriter - setOutputURL: (not implemented by this
    class), AVCaptureSession - startRunning (attach threw: Error: unable to intercept
    function at 0x15cea88a0; please file a bug), AVURLAsset - commonMetadata (not
    implemented by this class), AVURLAsset - metadata (not implemented by this class),
    PHAsset - localIdentifier (not implemented by this class), PHAsset - location (attach
    threw: Error: unable to intercept function at 0x15cea8480; please file a bug),
    PHPickerViewController - initWithConfiguration: (attach threw: Error: unable to
    intercept function at 0x15cea84f0; please file a bug). A hook that failed and a
    mechanism the app never used look identical from here, and only one of them is a
    finding.
  ▸ What was inside any of it. Destinations are captured at the socket, so TikTok's own
    traffic is included now, but the contents stay encrypted and this makes no attempt to
    open them.
  ▸ The public IP its servers recorded. That is observed at their end, not readable from the
    phone. The measured source address above tells you which connection carried the traffic
    that produced it.
  ▸ Location. The app made no location calls this run, which is not proof it never asks,
    only that it did not while being watched.
  ▸ Which of the values above rode along in which request. Reads and connections are both
    captured, but nothing ties a specific identifier to a specific outbound packet.
  ▸ Anything past the safety caps. The script stops recording new kinds of event once it
    hits its ceiling, so a runaway hook truncates this report instead of exhausting the
    machine running it.
  ▸ Anything the app never got round to. Watching, messaging or paying each open behaviour
    that never ran here.
